problem.text: Dave rolls a fair six-sided die until a six appears for the first time. Independently, Linda rolls a fair six-sided die until a six appears for the first time. Let $m$ and $n$ be relatively prime positive integers such that $\dfrac{m}{n}$ is the probability that the number of times Dave rolls his die is equal to or within one of the number of times Linda rolls her die. Find $m+n$.

steps.title: Where to start: the chance that the first six comes on roll $k$
steps.body:
Both players do the same thing, so first find one number: let $p_k$ be the probability that the first six comes on roll $k$. That needs $k - 1$ non-sixes and then a six.
$$p_k = \left(\tfrac{5}{6}\right)^{k-1}\cdot\tfrac{1}{6}$$

your_turn.answer: $p_1 = \frac{1}{6}$, $p_2 = \frac{5}{36}$, $p_3 = \frac{25}{216}$. Each is $\frac{5}{6}$ of the one before.

steps.title: Split on Dave's number of rolls
steps.body:
If Dave rolls $k$ times, Linda must roll $k - 1$, $k$ or $k + 1$ times. The two players are independent, so this case has probability $p_k(p_{k-1} + p_k + p_{k+1})$. Careful: when $k = 1$ Linda cannot roll $0$ times, so that first term is only $p_1(p_1 + p_2)$.
$$P = p_1(p_1+p_2) + p_2(p_1+p_2+p_3) + p_3(p_2+p_3+p_4) + \cdots$$

steps.title: The rest is a geometric series
steps.body: Going from the term for $k$ to the term for $k + 1$, the factor outside the brackets gets multiplied by $\frac{5}{6}$ and so does every $p$ inside the brackets. So from $k = 2$ on, each term is $\frac{5}{6}\cdot\frac{5}{6} = \frac{25}{36}$ times the one before, and the sum of those terms is $\dfrac{p_2(p_1+p_2+p_3)}{1 - \frac{25}{36}}$.

your_turn.prompt: Compute $p_2(p_1 + p_2 + p_3)$. (Hint: write $p_1 + p_2 + p_3$ over $216$.)
